[PAPER_0055, relevance_score=0.369] The Present Experiment

We make several predictions regarding performance in our task. For the incongruent-different composites (see Figure 1), we predict that d' will increase as the strength of evidence for a change in the target half increases (going from L to H). This prediction should hold in both the aligned and misaligned conditions. This is a manipulation check to ensure that discrimination of the target half is affected by the strength of the change.

[PAPER_0056, relevance_score=0.280] We predict that as the strength of evidence for a change in the distractor half (i.e., the bottom) increases (going from Same to Low to High), the false alarm rate will also increase. In the misaligned condition, the false alarm rate should not differ between composite types as the target half does not change and the distractor half should be easier to ignore. This is also a manipulation check to ensure that the effect of Congruency × Alignment interaction is sensitive to the strength of the interference.

[PAPER_0057, relevance_score=0.307] For the congruent-different composites, we predict that d' will increase as the strength of evidence for a change increases in both the target and distractor halves. The expected ordering from lowest to highest is L/L, L/H, H/L, H/H. Crucially, if no interference from the distractor half is present, it is expected that d' should be equivalent for the L target half composites (L/L and L/H) and for the H target half composites (H/L and H/H), which is also what we predict for the misaligned condition.

[PAPER_0058, relevance_score=0.293] This prediction reflects that the strength of the interference should affect the aligned condition but not the misaligned condition. For the misaligned condition, only the strength of the difference in the top half should matter.

Finally, we will assess the hallmark Congruency × Alignment interaction across the time course. If the composite face effect emerges, then d' should differ for L/L, L/H, H/L, and H/H between aligned and misaligned conditions; however, we make no predictions about when in the time course this will occur.

[PAPER_0060, relevance_score=0.216] Method

Participants

The first and second authors and a female student volunteer from the University of Melbourne completed 29 one-hour sessions. The volunteer was reimbursed $15 per hour. The average age was 23.7 (SD = 2.08) years, and all participants reported as right-handed and having normal or corrected-to-normal vision. We chose to collect many trials from a small number of participants as this provides a high level of precision at the level of the individual participant, individual stimulus, and individual response signal lag, appropriate for modeling of the SAT (Smith & Little, 2018).

[PAPER_0061, relevance_score=0.280] All participants completed two conditions: the aligned condition followed by the misaligned condition. The second author completed the experiment with no prior experience with the stimuli or method but was familiar with the hypotheses being tested. The volunteer was completely naïve to the purpose of the study. All testing was approved by the University of Melbourne Human Research Ethics Committee, approval ID number 1034866.16.

[PAPER_0069, relevance_score=0.233] Design and Procedure

Participants completed one training session and 28 experimental sessions (14 for each alignment condition) over several weeks. The training session consisted of six blocks of 78 trials with blank face templates, where the goal was to practice responding within 100 to 300 ms of the response signal, followed by four blocks of 78 trials making easy face discriminations (i.e., using only S/S and H/H composites).

Each experimental session consisted of ten blocks of 78 trials, equating to 780 trials.

[PAPER_0078, relevance_score=0.275] Results

Data Screening

The training session and the first block of each experimental session were considered practice and excluded from analysis. Responses made before the response signal, less than 100 ms after the response signal (i.e., anticipation errors), or more than 300 ms after the response signal were also excluded from analysis, resulting in 15.3% of the total data being removed. The percentage of trials included for each participant at each response signal lag in both conditions are shown in Table 1. It is clear that participants found it more difficult to respond within the time limit at early response signals.

[PAPER_0082, relevance_score=0.218] We additionally estimated the Bayesian SAT model without a hierarchical structure to each participant. Results of this analysis for each participant (plotted at each individual's total processing time) are provided in our online supplementary material . Group level inferences are given by examining the group level SAT parameter posteriors where appropriate.

These estimated values were compared between composite types and alignment conditions to determine differences in processing.

[PAPER_0080, relevance_score=0.341] SAT Function Analysis

Appendix A describes the details of our computational analysis. In short, we used a hierarchical Bayesian implementation of the SAT model with group-level distribution governing the parameters of the SAT function and individual level d' and criterion distributions across each response signal lag to provide likelihoods for the observed hit rates and false alarms rates. Plots of the SAT model for each composite type were used to examine how d' varied as a function of total processing time (i.e., response signal lag plus mean RT for that lag; see Table 2 for mean RTs).

[PAPER_0082, relevance_score=0.352] We additionally estimated the Bayesian SAT model without a hierarchical structure to each participant. Results of this analysis for each participant (plotted at each individual's total processing time) are provided in our online supplementary material . Group level inferences are given by examining the group level SAT parameter posteriors where appropriate.

[PAPER_0086, relevance_score=0.195] Effect of Discriminability: Bottom Half Same

We analyzed the effect of a change in the discriminability of the top half when the bottom half stayed the same (i.e., incongruent-different composite faces). The top two plots of Figure 6 display the 95% HDIs of the SAT functions and d' for when the incongruent-different composite faces were aligned (left) and misaligned (right). When faces were either aligned or misaligned and processing time exceeded 400 ms, the HDIs did not overlap for the L/S and H/S composite types.

[PAPER_0018, relevance_score=0.262] The first explanation is that if discriminations between faces (e.g., in a same-different judgment) are too difficult, then attention might need to be selectively deployed to specific features, breaking any Gestalt or configural processing (Blaha, 2017; Perry et al., 2010). Tasks which fail to show holistic processing may be using discriminations that do not allow for attention to the entire configuration or face template.

[PAPER_0019, relevance_score=0.258] For instance, composite faces often fail to show interference in categorization paradigms, such as the Garner tasks (Amishav & Kimchi, 2010; Fitousi, 2015; Richler et al., 2015) and related tasks (Cheng et al., 2018).

The second explanation is that holistic processing might take time to emerge. Processing might start as analytic or independent but through a gradual widening of attention, might become holistic (Fitousi, 2019).

[PAPER_0020, relevance_score=0.296] On the other hand, processing might start out as holistic and, over time, become more independent (cf., White et al., 2011). There is ample evidence that attention changes dynamically over the course of a trial (see, e.g., Sewell & Smith, 2012; Smith & Ratcliff, 2009). Tasks that fail to find holistic processing may not be assessing the same temporal location of processing as is assessed by the composite face task.

[PAPER_0025, relevance_score=0.354] For instance, measures of holistic processing based on the ordering of means across conditions are weaker than measures derived from strong inference methods (Platt, 1964; Smith & Little, 2018). In systems factorial technology (SFT; Little et al., 2017; Townsend & Nozawa, 1995), a set of methods and theoretically-based analyses are used to characterize different aspects of information processing.

[PAPER_0026, relevance_score=0.310] As defined by SFT, coactive processing, in which the top and bottom face halves are assumed to be pooled into a single object representation, most closely aligns with the idea of holism (Fifić et al., 2008; Wenger & Townsend, 2001). Coactivity can be contrasted with the independent processing of the top and the bottom face halves, either in serial (i.e., sequentially) or in parallel (i.e., simultaneously).

[PAPER_0027, relevance_score=0.376] These forms of processing generate nonparametric predictions that are based on mathematical proofs and methods, allowing for qualitative contrasts of each theory. For instance, Cheng et al. (2018) used systems factorial technology (Little et al., 2017; Townsend & Nozawa, 1995) to examine the processing of composite faces in a categorization task and found that composite faces are processed independently, with the top and bottom halves often processed serially.

[PAPER_0030, relevance_score=0.255] The SAT model captures the asymptotic or peak level of detection accuracy (measured in d'), as well as the dynamics of processing (McElree & Dosher, 1993) comprising the onset and the rate of processing. These three features are compared between composite types that differ in discriminability between the aligned and misaligned conditions to decompose any differences in processing. Several recent papers have also investigated the time course of composite face processing.

[PAPER_0038, relevance_score=0.270] Furthermore, if misaligning the face halves breaks holistic processing such that each half is processed as a distinct part, then congruency should have little to no effect. Consequently, a Congruency × Alignment interaction provides a standard for inferring holistic processing in the complete design (Richler & Gauthier, 2014). In addition, the complete design allows for the computation of a bias-free measure of decision accuracy via signal detection theory (Green & Swets, 1966; Macmillan & Creelman, 2005).

[PAPER_0042, relevance_score=0.278] Discrimination Difficulty and Holistic Processing

Perry et al. (2010) used a set of face morphs to examine whether processing exhibited supercapacity processing-a hallmark of coactivity, which, as we have argued above, should be considered a theoretically strong operationalization of holism since inference of supercapacity is based on nonparametric and qualitative contrasts allowing for strong inference (Platt, 1964; Smith & Little, 2018).

[PAPER_0044, relevance_score=0.258] We use a similar face morphing technique to Cheng et al. (2018) to obtain face halves of low and high discriminability (see Figure 3). A key question is whether the Congruency × Alignment interaction will appear at both levels of discriminability. It is possible that difficult discriminations, requiring attention to be directed to specific face parts, eliminate holistic processing (Blaha, 2017). On the other hand, discriminations that are too easy might be processed before any interference arises from the distractor face half.

[PAPER_0053, relevance_score=0.289] Yet integration of the top and bottom halves could occur either early in processing (i.e., faces are encoded holistically from the outset) or later in processing (i.e., holistic processing emerges from individually encoded top and bottom halves) in the composite task. For example, as pointed out by Meinhardt et al. (2014), diagnostic differences only modulate later ERP components, and recent investigations using RT distributions (Fitousi, 2019) have implicated the emergence of holism only later in processing. The SAT function also decomposes processing into different latent parameters.

[PAPER_0054, relevance_score=0.270] The SAT function also decomposes processing into different latent parameters. If interference slows down encoding, then we might expect to see differences in the rate of processing. Alternatively, differences could arise in the peak asymptotic level of processing interference once the entire composite has been encoded.

[PAPER_0059, relevance_score=0.262] If the difference is present early in the time course, this would support the early emergence of holistic processing, perhaps indicating that aligned faces are encoded holistically and are processed at a different rate to misaligned faces. By contrast, a later difference would support the late emergence of holistic processing, implicating interference arising over time. A strength of our method is that we can easily differentiate these two accounts.

[PAPER_0064, relevance_score=0.341] Twenty morph sets were then created by selecting four base faces (A, B, C, and D) at random, with replacement across sets, and morphing them together using a field morphing technique (see Steyvers, 1999) such that each morph set was a 3 × 3 matrix with variation between A and B forming one dimension and between C and D forming the other dimension (see Figure 3). Only the faces on the diagonals were used.

[PAPER_0065, relevance_score=0.258] Only the faces on the diagonals were used. On each trial, a top face half and a bottom face half were randomly drawn from the corner items of two morph sets to create a study composite face. Hence, from the 20 morph sets, there were 80 possible top face halves and 80 possible bottom face halves, yielding 6400 unique faces.

The presentation of a study face was always followed by a test face. Each half of the test face was drawn from the same morph set as the respective half of the study face.

[PAPER_0066, relevance_score=0.317] A test face half could be the same as the study face (S), differ by a low-discriminability change (L), or differ by a high discriminability change (H). In terms of the morph set in Figure 3, an L change is one step on both dimensions of the morph space (e.g., the top-left vs the center), and an H change is two steps on both dimensions (e.g., the top-left vs the bottom-right).

[PAPER_0074, relevance_score=0.257] Data Analysis

Changes in discriminability or d' were modeled as a function of the total time to process a given stimulus using the SAT model (Dosher, 1976; McElree & Dosher, 1993). This model has been used extensively to describe recognition memory processes in response signal paradigms (Dosher, 1976; McElree & Dosher, 1993; Ratcliff, 2006; Reed, 1973).

The parameters of this model and the resulting discriminability (d') and response bias (c) values at each response signal lag were estimated using Bayesian hierarchical modeling implemented in JAGS (Plummer, 2003). These estimated values were compared between composite types and alignment conditions to determine differences in processing.

[PAPER_0093, relevance_score=0.274] Congruency × Alignment Interaction

The hallmark of holistic processing in the composite face task is the Congruency × Alignment interaction in which congruency effects are diminished with misalignment. The top two plots of Figure 8 display the 95% Highest Density Intervals (HDIs) of the SAT functions and d' for all the congruent and incongruent composites faces at each level of discriminability when aligned (left) or misaligned (right).

[PAPER_0110, relevance_score=0.274] Theories of Holistic Processing

Numerous mechanisms have been proposed to give rise to holistic processing (Richler et al., 2012). The two most commonly supported are the template encoding, or Gestalt, hypothesis (Galton, 1883) and the attentional strategy hypothesis (Richler et al., 2012). Although it would be unwarranted to draw direct conclusions about any one mechanism based on the findings of a single behavioral experiment, we discuss which of these two theories our results align with the most.
